messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 20
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Pharmacist
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 69

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Visual (Water/Flooding): Water, flooding, or large bodies of water, Arguments: Arguments, Loss of Autonomy: Being forced to do something
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Dreams: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares, Avoid Similar People: Seeing other people that were involved in the event or that look similar, Punishment Thinking: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened
  Threat: Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
  Negative Appraisals: Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not

Vignette:
Akua's memories of her homeland are now inextricably linked with the sound of rushing water and the feeling of helplessness that comes with being trapped. It was during a brutal regime's crackdown on dissent that she was captured, tortured, and left for dead near a flooded riverbed. The specifics of those days remain fragmented, but the sensations – the feeling of her body contorted in impossible positions, the sound of her own screams echoing off the water – continue to haunt her. As a pharmacist in the United States, Akua is often required to work near water or navigate crowded areas, which now fill her with a sense of dread. Even the most mundane tasks can trigger vivid flashbacks: a customer's raised voice can transport her back to the interrogation room; the sight of a uniformed officer makes her heart racing as she frantically scans for an escape route. She has taken to avoiding confrontations at work, even when it means compromising patient care or her own professional development. Akua's relationship with her boyfriend, Kwame, is also strained due to her increasing withdrawal. He tries to be supportive, but she finds herself pushing him away whenever he touches her in certain ways or mentions anything related to their shared African heritage – the very things that used to bring them closer together. She avoids talking about the past, fearing that if she thinks about it too much, she won't be able to cope with the emotions that come flooding back. Akua's nights are fitful and anxious, spent scanning her darkened room for signs of danger or lying awake as she mentally maps out escape routes from every possible location. Her punishment thinking – a constant, gnawing voice that tells her she deserves to suffer – has become so ingrained that she often finds herself sabotaging her own attempts at self-care. Despite the incomplete picture in her mind, Akua's body remembers the traumatic events all too well. When memories resurface, she feels an intense physical response: her muscles tense, and she is transported back to the riverbank, reliving the helplessness and pain. Her inability to put these experiences into words leaves her feeling isolated, even from those closest to her. Kwame's recent concerns about their future together have brought Akua's avoidance strategies to a breaking point. She realizes that she can no longer continue living in this state of hypervigilance, always on edge and waiting for the next threat. Her guilt over surviving while others did not continues to weigh heavily on her mind, making it harder to shake off the feeling that she doesn't deserve happiness. It is this sense of desperation – a growing awareness that she cannot continue down this path alone – that has finally brought Akua to seek help. As she begins therapy, she fears that confronting these memories and emotions will overwhelm her, but hopes that by doing so, she might finally find some measure of peace and begin to rebuild her shattered life.
